messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Three years ago, a roadside detonation fractured Julian Vance’s deployment. He remembers the sudden concussive wave and the sight of his squad mates bleeding through torn fatigues, yet the experience refuses to cohere. His memories arrive as disjointed fragments—a shattered visor, a choked gasp, the smell of cordite—without any clear chronological image. When the full emotional weight of that day hits him, it comes as a raw, unanchored wave of terror that leaves him gasping on his living room floor. He has come to believe the experience was so extreme it could not have actually happened to him, a distant horror he feels he merely inhabited. Because his mind stored the trauma as unprocessed fragments rather than a narrative, ordinary stimuli like a colleague’s paper cut or a distant siren suddenly detonate as direct threats, pulling his focus entirely outward before he can rationalize them. Returning to his work as a social media manager, Julian found his civilian routine quickly eroded by the blast’s aftermath. When he rode in the passenger seat of his girlfriend’s car, the sudden braking of traffic mirrored the convoy’s ambush, and the auditory whine of the engine spiraled into the memory of rotor blades, immediately spiking his heart rate and making his palms sweat. That physiological alarm did not pass; it cemented his conviction that he was permanently altered for the worse, leaving the blast’s logic etched into his daily reality. To manage the escalating panic, he began rehearsing every work call and client meeting hours in advance, his mind pacing through polite pleasantries until the anxiety burned itself out. He also started avoiding any situation that required physical exertion, dropping his post-military running routine because the elevated heart rate felt indistinguishable from the panic that had nearly drowned him overseas. The more he isolated himself to avoid physical stress and mentally script his days, the more detached Julian felt from his own life. He told himself he had been fundamentally broken by the blast, that a properly trained soldier would never have frozen when the medic ran toward the burning Humvee. This sense of self-reproach made the external world feel profoundly foreign; he stopped seeing his fellow veterans as comrades, instead viewing them through a lens of isolation, convinced he was permanently an outsider who no longer belonged anywhere. Because he believed he was fundamentally flawed, his brain began cataloging every potential threat with renewed urgency. A distant ambulance siren or the sudden flash of brake lights would immediately pull his attention inward, reigniting the exact physiological alarm that had started the cycle. By retreating to a desk job and refusing to drive when others were passengers, he stripped away any context that might have diluted the alarm, leaving every sudden noise or visual cue to strike with unmitigated intensity. At his marketing agency, Julian managed campaigns from a corner desk, but the open floor plan kept his nervous system locked in readiness. When a junior designer bumped into his shoulder to get a file, Julian flinched violently, his breath catching as if struck. That involuntary physical reactivity forced him to retreat from shared office spaces, and he began avoiding screens that showed news footage or even stylized graphics with sharp angles, terrified that any visual cue resembling a laceration or contusion would unlock the flood of emotion. These avoidance habits did not calm his nerves; they only starved his brain of corrective experiences, ensuring the fragmented memories and the belief that his mind was permanently damaged continued to dictate his routine. Each time he retreated from physical exertion or scripted a conversation, his body remained locked in a state of readiness, unable to discharge the accumulated tension through normal regulation. Now, Julian’s apartment is quiet, but the silence is heavy with the weight of what he no longer does. He sleeps on the edge of the mattress, listening for rotor sounds in the night, certain that if he truly rested, he would miss the next threat. His girlfriend has grown distant, not from lack of care, but from the exhausting precision with which he anticipates and evades intimacy. He finally scheduled an intake appointment not because the panic subsided, but because the avoidance was costing him everything he wanted to keep. He is most afraid that the man who survived the blast is gone, replaced by someone permanently fractured, and he is hoping someone can show him how to bridge the gap between the horror he survived and the life he is trying to live.
